story_candidates.hed: Epsilon Eridani — the nearby star that made us listen
story_candidates.dek: A modest point in the River connects the first modern radio search for other civilizations with a nearby planetary system whose dust still challenges astronomers.
story_candidates.body:
Epsilon Eridani is about 10.5 light-years away. Its catalogue identity is HIP 16537, and its visual magnitude is about 3.7. It is a K-type star: cooler than the Sun, rather than a duplicate of it. The short distance makes it a useful place to investigate how planetary systems develop. In a dark sky you can see the star without an instrument; its planets and debris require very different observations. Sources: SIMBAD, https://simbad.cds.unistra.fr/simbad/sim-id?Ident=eps+Eri; NASA SOFIA account, https://science.nasa.gov/universe/exoplanets/sofia-confirms-nearby-planetary-system-is-similar-to-our-own/.

In 1960 Frank Drake pointed Green Bank's 85-foot Tatel radio telescope toward Epsilon Eridani and Tau Ceti for Project Ozma. The receiver searched near the 21-centimetre hydrogen line. Drake's own recollection describes the excitement when a pulsed signal appeared toward Epsilon Eridani. The observatory's history explains that the signal was terrestrial, associated with an airplane; the experiment found no evidence of another civilization. The lasting achievement was an experiment that turned a question into a measurable search. Sources: Green Bank Observatory, https://greenbankobservatory.org/about/telescopes/85-1-howard-tatel/; Frank Drake's reminiscence, https://www.gb.nrao.edu/fgdocs/tatel/ozma.htm.

Today the system has a known gas giant, Epsilon Eridani b. NASA's catalogue gives an orbital period of roughly 7.3 years and a distance of about 3.5 astronomical units from the star. Radial-velocity measurements detect the star's motion; they do not show a planet through an amateur eyepiece. The comparison with Jupiter concerns a giant planet and its orbit, not an established second Earth. Source: NASA exoplanet catalogue, https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/epsilon-eridani-b/.

Infrared observations reveal warm debris. A 2017 SOFIA study favoured material concentrated in at least one narrow belt over a broadly filled inner disk. That material traces collisions and the arrangement of smaller bodies. A later JWST/NIRCam study reported no statistically significant planetary point-source detection in its observations, while setting tighter limits on possible companions. Absence from those images does not cancel evidence from the star's motion. Sources: NASA SOFIA account, above; Llop-Sayson and colleagues, https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.08463.

To find the star, establish Orion and the winding Eridanus figure west of Rigel, then follow the labelled River stars to Epsilon on the finder. Its reference position is approximately 3h 33m, −9° 27′. At 45° N, the geometric upper culmination is about 36° above the southern horizon, calculated from declination. Begin with a wide field, confirm the surrounding pattern, then compare its warm colour with nearby stars. Neither the planet nor the dust belts are ordinary visual targets. Check the week's darkness and Moon interference separately. Identity and geometry: stored Hipparcos coordinates and accepted Star Almanack figure paths; https://simbad.cds.unistra.fr/simbad/sim-id?Ident=eps+Eri.

The historical setting matters. Project Ozma was not a search for an easily photographed spacecraft or a claim that a particular star had inhabitants. It tested whether a narrowband radio signal might stand out from natural background emission at a frequency chosen for physical reasons. A hydrogen-line search could be repeated and scrutinized, even when the result was null. Epsilon Eridani's proximity made it an intelligible early target, but proximity alone does not establish biology. The contrast between a disciplined radio experiment and the far more detailed planetary measurements available today gives the star its enduring place in the history of observation.

For a visual log, distinguish what the eye establishes from what instruments infer. Record whether Epsilon Eridani is visible directly, how readily it separates from neighbouring field stars, and the observing conditions. Its brightness and position are direct observing matters; a debris belt, a planet inferred from stellar motion, and a possible radio transmitter are separate scientific questions. Keeping those levels of evidence distinct is part of the story of this nearby star.

story_candidates.hed: Beta Reticuli — an orange giant with a hidden companion
story_candidates.dek: A naked-eye point in the southern Reticle conceals a stellar pair, while its far-southern position places it below the horizon for many northern observers.
story_candidates.body:
Beta Reticuli (β Ret) has visual magnitude about 3.84 and lies roughly 100 light-years away. Its visible component is an evolved orange K-type giant. A 2009 study adopted classification K2 IIIb and estimated a surface temperature of 4,580 kelvin and an age of 5–6 billion years. Older classifications called it a subgiant; its exact evolutionary status and age depend on stellar models.

The hidden companion reveals itself through periodic Doppler shifts in the giant’s spectral lines. The measured orbital period is about 1,918 days, or 5.25 years, with eccentricity 0.335. The study estimated a relative orbital semimajor axis of 3.53 astronomical units. One astronomical unit is the Earth–Sun distance; the semimajor axis describes the size of the elliptical orbit, not a constant spacing.

The companion is consistent with an M-type red dwarf. The estimated maximum apparent separation is only about 0.16 arcsecond, and the companion is much fainter: this is not an ordinary small-telescope double. The first orbital solution appeared in 1928, based on spectra collected during 1903–1925.

The orbit’s numbers make the hidden system easier to picture. Using the reported semimajor axis and eccentricity, the calculated separation ranges from about 2.35 astronomical units at closest approach to 4.71 at greatest separation. That is roughly the scale of the outer asteroid belt through the region approaching Jupiter’s orbit in our Solar System. This comparison describes distance, not planets: the orbit belongs to two stars. The separation we see projected on the sky also depends on the orbit’s orientation and the observing date.

The constellation is Reticulum, the Reticle. A reticle is a pattern of fine lines, such as crosshairs or a grid, placed in an instrument’s eyepiece to help aim it or measure positions. In an astronomical telescope, those lines provide a reference for measuring where stars appear; the constellation commemorates this measuring tool. Reticuli is the Latin genitive, meaning “of Reticulum.” Beta is its Greek-letter designation. Its southern position kept it outside the skies of many northern naming traditions, but that does not establish that southern cultures had no names for it.

Its reference position is approximately right ascension 3h 44m and declination −64° 48′. Geometrically, it never rises north of about 25.2° N, including the almanac’s default latitude of 45° N. South of about 25.2° S it is circumpolar. At 35° S it reaches about 60° altitude at upper culmination. These limits are calculated from declination, ignoring refraction and local obstructions; being above the horizon does not guarantee darkness.

For finding it, match Reticulum’s four-star figure to the chart. Beta is the pointed vertex where the sides from Alpha and Delta meet. Follow both sides to confirm the identification rather than selecting a star by brightness alone. Binoculars can help show the pattern and the giant’s warm colour; the close companion remains unresolved in an ordinary view.

The most rewarding ordinary observation is therefore the visible giant in its surrounding pattern. First use a wide field to establish the figure, then compare Beta’s colour with nearby stars. A telescope can make the star brighter to the eye, but magnification alone cannot overcome the close companion’s tiny spacing and strong contrast. Seeing a single point is entirely consistent with the scientific evidence for two stars. The star’s spectrum and changing motion reveal information that its visual appearance does not.

This account describes the system and its enduring observing geometry. Check the current week and your location for darkness, culmination time, Moon interference and any nearby planet. A planet beside Beta is a temporary visitor, not a permanent member of the pattern.

Sources: Ramm, Pourbaix, Hearnshaw & Komonjinda (2009), “Spectroscopic orbits for K giants β Reticuli and ν Octantis,” Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society 394, 1695–1710, doi:10.1111/j.1365-2966.2009.14459.x (https://academic.oup.com/mnras/article/394/3/1695/1072315); IAU constellation names (https://iauarchive.eso.org/public/themes/constellations/). Finder instructions and geometric visibility calculations are original Star Almanack work based on the accepted chart and catalogue coordinates.

story_candidates.hed: IC 342 — a neighbouring galaxy behind our own curtain
story_candidates.dek: The Hidden Galaxy spans roughly a full Moon on the sky, yet foreground dust and its spread-out light make it a patient telescope target.
story_candidates.body:
Caldwell 5 and IC 342 name the same spiral galaxy in Camelopardalis, the Giraffe. At roughly 11 million light-years away it is close enough for detailed study, but our own Milky Way obstructs the view. Foreground stars and dust crowd this direction, dimming and confusing the galaxy's light. The nickname Hidden Galaxy describes that intervening curtain; it does not mean that the galaxy lacks stars. Source: NASA's Caldwell catalogue, https://science.nasa.gov/mission/hubble/science/explore-the-night-sky/hubble-caldwell-catalog/caldwell-5/.

British amateur astronomer William Frederick Denning discovered the object in the early 1890s. Its later Caldwell designation is an observing-list identity. When comparing charts, use the IC number to keep the physical galaxy distinct from its place in a particular list. NASA recommends clear, dark conditions and a telescope; haze and city light make the search harder. Source: NASA's Caldwell catalogue, above.

Euclid showed why a change of wavelength helps. Its near-infrared observations penetrate the foreground dust more effectively and measure light from cool, low-mass stars. The wide image covers the galaxy while retaining enough detail to identify stars and star clusters. This makes it possible to examine a whole external spiral, rather than only a small central field. Our position inside the Milky Way makes that outside perspective valuable. Source: ESA, Euclid's view of IC 342, https://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Science/Euclid/Euclid_s_view_of_spiral_galaxy_IC_342.

The galaxy also contains unusually bright X-ray sources. NASA's 2013 NuSTAR account describes two sources much brighter than typical stellar-mass black holes. Their masses and the reason for their brightness required further investigation; the image alone did not settle the question. Different wavelengths answer different questions: infrared can reveal obscured stellar structure, while X-rays trace energetic processes around compact objects. A telescope's quiet smudge can therefore contain activity that visible observing does not reveal. Source: NASA/JPL, https://science.nasa.gov/photojournal/blazing-black-holes-spotted-in-spiral-beauty/.

For the visual search, establish Camelopardalis between the familiar northern landmarks and match its blue stick figure on the finder. Locate the yellow target circle near right ascension 3h 47m and declination +68° 06′, using the adjacent plotted stars to confirm the field. These are reference coordinates, not a prediction of a visible spiral pattern. At 45° N the galaxy is circumpolar and reaches about 67° altitude at upper culmination, calculated geometrically from declination. Start at low magnification and look for extended, faint light. Its total magnitude collects light from a large area, so it cannot be compared directly with the ease of seeing a star of similar magnitude. Expect a subtle galaxy, not the colour and detail of a space-telescope photograph. Position and finding geometry: stored Caldwell coordinates and accepted Star Almanack figure paths. Weekly Moon and transparency conditions remain separate.

IC 342 is an especially useful lesson in the difference between integrated brightness and surface brightness. The total light of a galaxy is spread across an extended patch rather than concentrated into a point. Foreground extinction dims that light further, and a bright sky can erase the already weak contrast. An observer who fails to see the galaxy has not contradicted its catalogue magnitude. The result depends on sky darkness, transparency, field identification, aperture and the ability to notice a broad, low-contrast glow.

The galaxy also illustrates why different observing techniques produce different portraits of the same object. Visible-light images contend with intervening Milky Way dust. Infrared measurements can reveal more of the hidden stellar structure, while X-ray observations identify energetic sources that would not stand out in a visual eyepiece. These observations complement rather than replace one another. The appropriate backyard goal is modest: verify the correct field and, under suitable conditions, look for the galaxy's diffuse central light. Spiral detail and individual energetic sources belong to very different observing regimes.

story_candidates.hed: Pleiades — a familiar cluster with a much larger family
story_candidates.dek: The Seven Sisters offer a wide-field view of young stars, passing dust and a stellar family whose known extent has grown far beyond the familiar little pattern.
story_candidates.body:
The Pleiades, Messier 45, are an open star cluster in Taurus, roughly 440 light-years away. An open cluster is a group of stars associated through their birth and gravity, rather than a chance outline drawn between unrelated stars. The bright points visible to the unaided eye are only its most conspicuous members. NASA’s Hubble Messier catalogue gives the cluster an integrated visual magnitude of 1.6 and describes more than a thousand members. Integrated magnitude combines their light; it is not the magnitude of every star or a promise that faint nebulosity will be easy to see. Source: NASA, Messier 45, https://science.nasa.gov/mission/hubble/science/explore-the-night-sky/hubble-messier-catalog/messier-45/.

This grouping has been observed since antiquity and has no single known discoverer. Its catalogue designation does not mean that Messier discovered it. Galileo’s telescopic observations revealed stars beyond the familiar unaided-eye pattern. What looks like a small handful becomes a much richer field when an instrument collects more light. The historical Seven Sisters name describes a cultural pattern; it is not an astronomical count of the cluster’s population. Source: NASA’s Hubble Messier catalogue, above.

The stars are young on the scale of stellar evolution, with an age of roughly 100 million years. Their surrounding dust was once interpreted as leftover material from their formation. NASA’s WISE account explains why that is unlikely: radiation and stellar winds should have dispersed the original material by this age. The cluster is probably passing through interstellar dust. In visible photographs, some of that dust scatters starlight toward us, making reflection nebulosity. The dust does not have to generate its own visible light to appear luminous in the picture. Source: NASA/JPL-Caltech, Seven Sisters Get WISE, https://science.nasa.gov/photojournal/seven-sisters-get-wise/.

Infrared pictures tell a complementary story. WISE detects emission from warm dust as well as stellar light. Its published colours encode different infrared wavelengths; they are not the colours an observer would see through an eyepiece. A blue visible reflection cloud and red-coded infrared dust can represent different observations of the same region. Before comparing a photograph with the visual view, check what wavelengths and display colours the image uses. Source: NASA/JPL-Caltech’s WISE account, above.

The familiar cluster is also part of a much more extended proposed family. In November 2025, NASA reported a study identifying more than 3,000 associated stars across about 1,900 light-years, called the Greater Pleiades Complex. Researchers combined Galactic motions, stellar rotation and chemical abundances. Rotation provided an age clue because stars generally slow as they age; similar chemistry offered another test of shared origins. This is evidence for a dispersed stellar population, not a claim that a backyard view suddenly contains three times as many bright Sisters. The interpretation can be refined by later observations. Source: NASA, NASA’s TESS Spacecraft Triples Size of Pleiades Star Cluster, https://science.nasa.gov/missions/tess/nasas-tess-spacecraft-triples-size-of-pleiades-star-cluster/.

For finding the cluster, begin with Orion’s Belt, follow its line toward orange Aldebaran and the Hyades V, then continue in the same general direction to the compact Pleiades grouping. Match the chart’s whole arrangement. A wide binocular field preserves the cluster’s context; high magnification can crop the pattern and make recognition harder. The stars are much easier visual targets than their faint surrounding dust. A photographic blue veil is not a reliable expectation for an ordinary glance through binoculars.

Let the weekly almanac supply the changing conditions: darkness, Moon interference, altitude and any nearby planet. The stored cluster story remains useful when those conditions change. A planet crossing this field is a visitor in projection; it does not belong to the cluster. Finding instructions here are original Star Almanack wording based on the accepted guide-star route.

At roughly 11 million light-years away it is close enough for detailed study, but our own Milky Way obstructs the view. Foreground stars and dust crowd this direction, dimming and confusing the galaxy's light. The nickname Hidden Galaxy describes that intervening curtain; it does not mean that the galaxy lacks stars. Source: NASA's Caldwell catalogue, https://science.nasa.gov/mission/hubble/science/explore-the-night-sky/hubble-caldwell-catalog/caldwell-5/.

British amateur astronomer William Frederick Denning discovered the object in the early 1890s. Its later Caldwell designation is an observing-list identity. When comparing charts, use the IC number to keep the physical galaxy distinct from its place in a particular list. NASA recommends clear, dark conditions and a telescope; haze and city light make the search harder. Source: NASA's Caldwell catalogue, above.

Euclid showed why a change of wavelength helps. Its near-infrared observations penetrate the foreground dust more effectively and measure light from cool, low-mass stars. The wide image covers the galaxy while retaining enough detail to identify stars and star clusters. This makes it possible to examine a whole external spiral, rather than only a small central field. Our position inside the Milky Way makes that outside perspective valuable. Source: ESA, Euclid's view of IC 342, https://www.esa.int/Science_Exploration/Space_Science/Euclid/Euclid_s_view_of_spiral_galaxy_IC_342.

The galaxy also contains unusually bright X-ray sources. NASA's 2013 NuSTAR account describes two sources much brighter than typical stellar-mass black holes. Their masses and the reason for their brightness required further investigation; the image alone did not settle the question. Different wavelengths answer different questions: infrared can reveal obscured stellar structure, while X-rays trace energetic processes around compact objects. A telescope's quiet smudge can therefore contain activity that visible observing does not reveal. Source: NASA/JPL, https://science.nasa.gov/photojournal/blazing-black-holes-spotted-in-spiral-beauty/.

For the visual search, establish Camelopardalis between the familiar northern landmarks and match its blue stick figure on the finder. Locate the yellow target circle near right ascension 3h 47m and declination +68° 06′, using the adjacent plotted stars to confirm the field. These are reference coordinates, not a prediction of a visible spiral pattern. At 45° N the galaxy is circumpolar and reaches about 67° altitude at upper culmination, calculated geometrically from declination. Start at low magnification and look for extended, faint light. Its total magnitude collects light from a large area, so it cannot be compared directly with the ease of seeing a star of similar magnitude. Expect a subtle galaxy, not the colour and detail of a space-telescope photograph. Position and finding geometry: stored Caldwell coordinates and accepted Star Almanack figure paths. Weekly Moon and transparency conditions remain separate.

IC 342 is an especially useful lesson in the difference between integrated brightness and surface brightness. The total light of a galaxy is spread across an extended patch rather than concentrated into a point. Foreground extinction dims that light further, and a bright sky can erase the already weak contrast. An observer who fails to see the galaxy has not contradicted its catalogue magnitude. The result depends on sky darkness, transparency, field identification, aperture and the ability to notice a broad, low-contrast glow.

The galaxy also illustrates why different observing techniques produce different portraits of the same object. Visible-light images contend with intervening Milky Way dust. Infrared measurements can reveal more of the hidden stellar structure, while X-ray observations identify energetic sources that would not stand out in a visual eyepiece. These observations complement rather than replace one another. The appropriate backyard goal is modest: verify the correct field and, under suitable conditions, look for the galaxy's diffuse central light. Spiral detail and individual energetic sources belong to very different observing regimes.

stories.hed: Pleiades — a familiar cluster with a much larger family
stories.dek: The Seven Sisters offer a wide-field view of young stars, passing dust and a stellar family whose known extent has grown far beyond the familiar little pattern.
stories.body:
The Pleiades, Messier 45, are an open star cluster in Taurus, roughly 440 light-years away. An open cluster is a group of stars associated through their birth and gravity, rather than a chance outline drawn between unrelated stars. The bright points visible to the unaided eye are only its most conspicuous members. NASA’s Hubble Messier catalogue gives the cluster an integrated visual magnitude of 1.6 and describes more than a thousand members. Integrated magnitude combines their light; it is not the magnitude of every star or a promise that faint nebulosity will be easy to see. Source: NASA, Messier 45, https://science.nasa.gov/mission/hubble/science/explore-the-night-sky/hubble-messier-catalog/messier-45/.

This grouping has been observed since antiquity and has no single known discoverer. Its catalogue designation does not mean that Messier discovered it. Galileo’s telescopic observations revealed stars beyond the familiar unaided-eye pattern. What looks like a small handful becomes a much richer field when an instrument collects more light. The historical Seven Sisters name describes a cultural pattern; it is not an astronomical count of the cluster’s population. Source: NASA’s Hubble Messier catalogue, above.

The stars are young on the scale of stellar evolution, with an age of roughly 100 million years. Their surrounding dust was once interpreted as leftover material from their formation. NASA’s WISE account explains why that is unlikely: radiation and stellar winds should have dispersed the original material by this age. The cluster is probably passing through interstellar dust. In visible photographs, some of that dust scatters starlight toward us, making reflection nebulosity. The dust does not have to generate its own visible light to appear luminous in the picture. Source: NASA/JPL-Caltech, Seven Sisters Get WISE, https://science.nasa.gov/photojournal/seven-sisters-get-wise/.

Infrared pictures tell a complementary story. WISE detects emission from warm dust as well as stellar light. Its published colours encode different infrared wavelengths; they are not the colours an observer would see through an eyepiece. A blue visible reflection cloud and red-coded infrared dust can represent different observations of the same region. Before comparing a photograph with the visual view, check what wavelengths and display colours the image uses. Source: NASA/JPL-Caltech’s WISE account, above.

The familiar cluster is also part of a much more extended proposed family. In November 2025, NASA reported a study identifying more than 3,000 associated stars across about 1,900 light-years, called the Greater Pleiades Complex. Researchers combined Galactic motions, stellar rotation and chemical abundances. Rotation provided an age clue because stars generally slow as they age; similar chemistry offered another test of shared origins. This is evidence for a dispersed stellar population, not a claim that a backyard view suddenly contains three times as many bright Sisters. The interpretation can be refined by later observations. Source: NASA, NASA’s TESS Spacecraft Triples Size of Pleiades Star Cluster, https://science.nasa.gov/missions/tess/nasas-tess-spacecraft-triples-size-of-pleiades-star-cluster/.

For finding the cluster, begin with Orion’s Belt, follow its line toward orange Aldebaran and the Hyades V, then continue in the same general direction to the compact Pleiades grouping. Match the chart’s whole arrangement. A wide binocular field preserves the cluster’s context; high magnification can crop the pattern and make recognition harder. The stars are much easier visual targets than their faint surrounding dust. A photographic blue veil is not a reliable expectation for an ordinary glance through binoculars.

Let the weekly almanac supply the changing conditions: darkness, Moon interference, altitude and any nearby planet. The stored cluster story remains useful when those conditions change. A planet crossing this field is a visitor in projection; it does not belong to the cluster. Finding instructions here are original Star Almanack wording based on the accepted guide-star route.
